Transcript: So - the standard story about common-pool resources. You've all met it. Hardin's parable: a pasture open to all, each herder adds one more animal because the gain is private and the cost is shared, and the pasture is stripped bare. Ruin, he said, is the destination toward which all men rush. Tidy. Memorable. And, um, in a narrow sense unobjectionable - the arithmetic does work, given the assumptions.

But notice what those assumptions do. The herders in the parable cannot talk to one another. They cannot make a rule, cannot monitor a neighbour, cannot impose so much as a mild sanction. Which means the model quietly begs the question - it assumes away exactly the institutions whose existence is at issue, and then reports their absence as a discovery. Now, I want to be careful here. This is not to say the parable is wrong. Where users really are anonymous and mobile - high-seas fisheries are the obvious case - the outcome Hardin describes is not just possible, it is routine.

The complication comes from the fieldwork. Ostrom and her colleagues catalogued Swiss alpine pastures, Japanese village forests, Spanish irrigation systems, some of them governed for six or seven centuries without either privatisation or a state. And what they found was not harmony. Cheating, disputes, sanctions, all present. What was also present were graduated penalties, boundaries everybody recognised, and cheap local ways of settling quarrels.

So where does that leave the parable? Not discarded, I would say. Rescued as a special case - the case where communication has been ruled out in advance. And here is the awkward part for policy: for much of the twentieth century governments read Hardin as licence to nationalise or to privatise, and in doing so dismantled working local arrangements they had never bothered to study. That lesson was expensive.
prompt: [Academic Talk — Institutional Economics] What is the lecturer's attitude toward Hardin's parable of the pasture?
choices: He treats its reasoning as sound but its reach as overstated, and keeps it for a narrow class of cases.
He holds that its central calculation is mistaken, since the private gain does not in fact exceed the shared cost.
He accepts it as a general law of resource use that the fieldwork has since confirmed in detail.
He rejects it outright, on the grounds that the fieldwork found no cheating or disputes among users.
correct_answer: He treats its reasoning as sound but its reach as overstated, and keeps it for a narrow class of cases.
explanation: C1 stance work: the lecturer never evaluates the parable directly, so the answer must be assembled from 'in a narrow sense unobjectionable', 'this is not to say the parable is wrong', and 'rescued as a special case'. B contradicts his explicit concession that the arithmetic works; C ignores that he confines the parable to anonymous, mobile users; D misreports the fieldwork, which found cheating and disputes were present.

Transcript: Right - so, the headline says coffee drinkers live longer. And the study behind it is not junk. Large sample, careful follow-up, and the association is there and it is fairly strong. The question I want to press is what that association is made of.

Start with the obvious worry: confounding. Coffee drinkers in that cohort were also, on average, wealthier, better housed, more likely to hold a desk job. Any of those will do the work the coffee is being credited with. Fine - the analysts knew that. They adjusted for income, occupation, exercise, smoking. And after adjustment the association shrank. But it did not disappear.

Now, at this point a great many people conclude that the residue must be causal - whatever survives adjustment is the real effect. And that inference is, I am afraid, wishful. Adjustment removes only what you measured, and it removes it only as well as you measured it. Smoking in that questionnaire was recorded as yes or no. Half a pack a day and two packs a day went into the same box. So what is left over need not be a coffee effect at all; it may be the part of smoking your instrument was too blunt to catch. An artifact, in other words - a fact about the measuring, not about the world.

Does that make observational work worthless? No, and I would resist that conclusion strongly. There are cases where something outside the correlation is doing the argumentative work. Where nature has done the randomising for us. Where the association reverses inside every subgroup. Where the dose tracks the response too cleanly for a confounder to mimic. Those are informative.

So the discipline here is not blanket scepticism about correlations. It is asking, every single time, what would have to be true of the world for this pattern to arise without the cause you have in mind.
prompt: [Academic Talk — Epidemiology] How does the lecturer regard the claim that whatever survives statistical adjustment is the real effect?
choices: As a sound rule of thumb, provided the list of measured confounders is long enough.
As an understandable but unsafe conclusion, because adjustment is limited by how coarsely the confounders were recorded.
As a sign that the direction of causation has been reversed, with health driving coffee consumption.
As evidence that statistical adjustment should be abandoned in favour of laboratory work.
correct_answer: As an understandable but unsafe conclusion, because adjustment is limited by how coarsely the confounders were recorded.
explanation: Stance is carried by 'a great many people conclude' plus the hedged 'I am afraid, wishful' and the immediate reason about the yes/no smoking variable. A is the position he is rejecting, restated with a qualifier; C names a possibility the talk never raises; D overshoots his explicit refusal to call observational work worthless.

passage:
Transcript: Two accounts of the same riot, written in the same month, and they do not agree. One is a magistrate's report to the capital. The other is a letter from a merchant to his brother. The temptation - and it is a strong one - is to ask which of the two men was more honest. That is almost never the productive question.

Ask instead what each document was for. The magistrate is explaining, to superiors who may punish him, why order broke down on his watch. He has every reason to inflate the crowd: a mob of two thousand excuses what a scuffle of forty does not. The merchant is warning his brother whether to send goods next season. He has reason to exaggerate the danger too, but a different reason - and, this matters, no reason whatever to describe the magistrate as competent. Yet he does. That remark cuts against the grain of his own interest, and for exactly that reason it is worth more than the sentences on either side of it.

Now, the older method - sift the sources, decide which one is reliable, then believe it throughout - is not so much wrong as far too coarse. Reliability is not a property of a document. It is a property of a document with respect to a particular claim. A thoroughly partisan chronicler may be useless on motive and excellent on weather.

One more caution before we stop. Where the silences agree, be careful. Neither writer mentions the militia. It is tempting to conclude that the militia never came. But the magistrate would hardly advertise having summoned them, and the merchant may simply not have known. Absence of mention, here, is evidence about what was sayable, not about what occurred. Silences have authors too.
prompt: [Academic Talk — Historiography] What is the lecturer's view of the older method of ranking sources by reliability?
choices: He regards it as discredited, since documents written for a superior are systematically false.
He endorses it, provided the historian first determines which of the two writers was the more honest.
He shares its aim but faults it for assigning reliability to whole documents instead of to particular claims.
He objects that it ignores the purposes for which documents were written, which is the only thing now recoverable.
correct_answer: He shares its aim but faults it for assigning reliability to whole documents instead of to particular claims.
explanation: The judgement lives in one concessive formula - 'not so much wrong as far too coarse' - and in the chronicler who is useless on motive but excellent on weather. A hardens a predicted bias into blanket falsity; B revives the honesty question he has just set aside; D adds an 'only' the talk contradicts by recovering more than purposes.

Transcript: Here is a puzzle out of the radiology literature. Two readers work through the same set of scans, and one of them catches more tumours than the other. The obvious conclusion is that she is the better reader. Sharper eyes. Hold that thought.

Because she also flags more scans that turn out to be perfectly clean. And once you know that, the obvious conclusion is in trouble. Detecting a faint signal in noise involves two quite separate things, and the old way of scoring - count the hits - runs them together. There is how distinguishable the signal is from the noise for that observer; call it sensitivity. And there is where the observer puts the line at which she is willing to say yes, I see it. That is the criterion. Two different quantities. Slide the criterion toward yes and your hits go up - and your false alarms go up with them, in lockstep. You have not seen any better. You have only become readier to say so.

So our radiologist may be more sensitive. Or she may simply be moving the goalposts, and I mean that neutrally, which is not how the phrase is ordinarily used. There is no fault in it. Where a missed tumour costs a life and a false alarm costs a second scan, shifting the line is exactly the rational thing to do.

And this is where I would push back a little on the textbook framing, which treats the criterion as a nuisance parameter - something to be estimated and set aside so that sensitivity can be read off cleanly. In the laboratory, fine. In a hospital, the criterion is not noise in the measurement. It is the clinical judgement. It encodes what the institution takes a mistake to be worth. Strip it out and you have measured the eye while throwing away the decision.
prompt: [Academic Talk — Psychophysics] What is the lecturer's position on the textbook practice of treating the criterion as a nuisance parameter?
choices: He considers it a statistical error that inflates estimates of sensitivity.
He accepts it wherever the two kinds of error carry unequal costs.
He rejects it, holding that sensitivity cannot be estimated separately from the criterion at all.
He allows it as a laboratory convenience but denies it where the two kinds of error carry unequal costs.
correct_answer: He allows it as a laboratory convenience but denies it where the two kinds of error carry unequal costs.
explanation: The stance is built from 'push back a little', the concession 'in the laboratory, fine', and the contrasting hospital case; it is never stated as approval or rejection. A misreads a framing choice as a computational mistake; B inverts exactly the condition he sets; C denies the separation the whole talk depends on.

Transcript: When the big replication projects reported back - psychology first, then economics, then cancer biology - the number everybody fixed on was the headline rate. Something under half. And the immediate explanation, in the press at least, was misconduct. Somebody had been cooking the books.

I want to suggest that is the least interesting explanation available, and probably the smallest contributor. Fraud exists. It is rare, and when it is caught it is caught precisely because it is crude.

The bigger problem is subtler and requires nobody to lie. Think about a single honest analysis. Do you exclude the participants who responded implausibly fast? Do you log-transform the skewed variable? Do you keep the two conditions apart or pool them? Every one of those choices is defensible. Every one of them was made after the data had arrived. Gelman calls this the garden of forking paths - and notice, the researcher walks down only one path. She never runs twenty analyses and reports the prettiest. She runs one, honestly. But which one she ran depended on what she saw, and that dependence inflates her false-positive rate just as surely as fishing would.

Now, a qualification, because the crisis narrative has hardened into something rather too simple. A failed replication is not a refutation. It may mean the effect is absent. It may mean the effect is real but small, or fragile, or bounded by some feature of the original setting that the second laboratory did not reproduce. Telling those apart is genuinely hard, and the loudest voices on both sides tend to skate past it.

Still - and I do not want the qualification to swallow the point - the direction of the correction is not in doubt. In the fields that began pre-registering their analyses, published effect sizes fell. Which is what you would expect if forking paths, and not fraud, had been doing the inflating all along.

As the principal cause, though one that is difficult to demonstrate case by case.

Transcript: The standard picture - and it is a powerful one - puts the environment on one side, posing problems, and the organism on the other, adapting or failing to. Selection is what the world does to a lineage.

Earthworms make that picture uncomfortable. Their physiology is, frankly, a poor match for soil. The kidney they inherited is a freshwater kidney, built for a life their ancestors left behind. And they have not evolved a soil kidney. What they have done instead is remake the soil - burrowing, casting, dragging leaf litter down after them - until the ground immediately around them is wet enough for a freshwater kidney to work in. So which side is doing the adapting?

Odling-Smee and others call this niche construction, and the term I want you to hold on to is ecological inheritance. An earthworm hatches into a burrow system its grandparents dug. It inherits genes from its parents and, quite separately, it inherits a modified world. Some of the selection pressures acting on it were built by its own ancestors. The arrow runs both ways.

Now, how much does this actually change? Here I would be cautious. The critics - Laland's opponents, and they are not fools - point out that standard theory can absorb these cases without strain. A beaver dam is environmental change; call the changed environment a selection pressure, and the bookkeeping still comes out right. And that is fair, as far as it goes. My own view, for what it is worth, is that this is less a refutation of the older account than a complaint about what that account makes easy to notice. A framework that treats the environment as external will keep generating questions in which the organism is the passive party. You can add the feedback loop afterwards. Whether you would ever have thought to look for it is another matter.

He agrees with them that niche construction adds nothing worth recording to the older account.
He concedes that their technical point holds and objects only that their framework directs attention badly.
He argues that standard theory has no way of representing feedback from organism to environment.
correct_answer: He concedes that their technical point holds and objects only that their framework directs attention badly.

Transcript: Take something as unglamorous as temperature. Before you can measure it, you need a thermometer. To know that your thermometer is any good, you need to know that mercury expands uniformly as temperature rises. And to know that, you would have to measure temperature - independently - which is precisely what you do not yet have.

Hasok Chang calls this the problem of nomic measurement, and it is not a puzzle you can dissolve by being more careful. There is no observation that breaks the circle from outside. Fahrenheit could not check his mercury against the truth. There was no such gauge to check it against.

So how did the thing ever get settled? Not by finding a foundation. By pulling itself up by its own bootstraps - and I use that phrase in its awkward original sense, not the cheerful modern one about self-reliance. The procedure looks impossible from outside and works anyway. You assume the mercury behaves. You build the scale. You use the scale to state laws - the gas laws, latent heat. Those laws then tell you where mercury ought to misbehave, and off you go to look. Mostly it does not. Where it does, you correct, or you switch to another substance, and you run the loop again.

Notice what that is and is not. It is not proof. Nothing here rests on bedrock. But it is not idle either. A bad starting assumption does not stay hidden; it makes the resulting laws messy, and the mess accumulates until somebody trips over it. Self-correction without foundations. Now, some philosophers take all this as licence for a fairly relaxed conventionalism - the scale is simply a choice, so nothing is really being tracked. I would resist that. The choice was constrained at every turn by whether the physics you got out of it hung together, and that constraint did most of the work.

He treats it as irrelevant, because the philosophers proposing it have ignored the historical record.
He grants the premise it starts from but holds that it draws far too much from it.
correct_answer: He grants the premise it starts from but holds that it draws far too much from it.
explanation: The stance turns on a bare 'I would resist that' plus the reason that follows about constraint, set against his own earlier admission that no external check exists. A takes the shared premise for agreement with the conclusion; B has him retracting the circle he spent the talk establishing; C invents a charge he never makes.

Transcript: Rent in central Seoul, or London, or the Bay Area is punishing. Firms pay it. Workers pay it. If you take the cost-minimising firm of the textbook seriously, this should not be happening - you would move to where land is cheap. Some do. Most do not. So something is being bought with that rent.

Marshall's answer, from the 1890s, came in three parts, and it has held up remarkably well. First, suppliers: a cluster can support specialists no single firm could keep busy on its own. Second, matching. A worker with a peculiar skill needs the one employer who happens to need it; in a thin market she never finds him, and both of them settle for less than they might have had. Third, and much the vaguest, knowledge spillovers - things overheard, people who change firms, ideas that leak across a wall.

Now, the third is where I would urge some caution. It has become the fashionable explanation, partly, I suspect, because it flatters the industries doing the explaining. And the evidence is real but indirect. Patent citations cluster geographically, more than chance would predict. That is suggestive. It is not decisive, because firms that had already clustered for the first two reasons would generate the very same citation pattern.

There is also a selection problem nobody has fully solved. Are productive workers made productive by the city, or does the city simply collect the people who were going to be productive anyway? Studies that follow individuals as they move do find a genuine gain. But they find a gain that arrives gradually, over years - which sits awkwardly with the overhearing story and rather better with the matching one.

None of which makes spillovers a myth. It makes the point that we have been reading the strongest evidence in support of the weakest of the three mechanisms.
